escalations.situation: All 24 containers preview eligible with zero blockers, but the 24 plans together schedule 684 copy operations over 139 distinct files (~16.6 MB) into dev/archive/: 56 adopter docs under docs/, 44 .jit/.github/scripts/mcp-server files, 29 dev/ files, 6 production sources under crates/, and 4 repository-root files including README.md and AGENTS.md. Predicted at planning time — seven issue descriptions say '90 for copying' — so this is not a regression; the counts have drifted up (132/92/91 vs 90) because docs/ grew since.
escalations.lead_analysis: The classifier selects an action from two independent booleans at artifact_classifier.rs:765: (wants_destination, needs_source) -> Copy/Move/Retain. 'Permanent' was designed for dev/architecture — living documentation the archive wants a frozen snapshot of while readers keep the live file — so it sets needs_source=true and Copy falls out. D-14 needed out-of-root artifacts to stop BLOCKING and expressed that by extending is_permanent() to cover anything outside the development root (:129-137). That flag only says keep the source; wants_destination stays true. The copying is an inherited side effect rather than a chosen behaviour. Epic REQ-14 requires only that no unmanaged-selected-root blocker is reported and that no file outside the development root is relocated — it does not require copying, so classifying out-of-root sources to the existing Retain action satisfies it just as literally.
options: A: classify out-of-root sources Retain (684 copies -> 8); configured permanent roots keep Copy. Costs an amendment to D-14's recorded mechanism, a remediation task against 4f9af089's shipped classification, and a re-preview of the 12 affected containers.
B: execute as planned, as the reviewed plan and breakdown review approved.
C: unlink the out-of-root documents first — explicitly rejected by D-14 as destroying traceability from ten terminal issues.
escalations.lead_recommendation: A. It matches what D-14 was trying to buy, and B risks a finding at the epic's own holistic-review gate against @/inv/single-source-prose ('a hand-maintained copy is a staleness defect') and @/charter/D-13, both cited as binding in the epic's Notes — seven frozen copies of the adopter docs tree are exactly that.

(1) Bound the discovery closure at a permanent/out-of-root node instead of walking through it; (2) classify out-of-root sources to the existing Retain action. Projected 684 copies -> 20; all 175 relocations preserved (simulated per container against each plan's edge graph, zero moves lost). Filed as 0e5dff57 under story:area-classification with satisfies:REQ-14, wired ahead of all 24 sweeps. D-14's recorded mechanism amended in the epic description; the 15 [hard] criteria are untouched and REQ-14 still holds literally.
escalations.measurement: Root cause is NOT hand-made doc links: the 24 containers carry 236 explicitly linked documents between them, and the worst container has 4 explicit roots yielding 91 embedded artifacts. artifact_discovery.rs:303-338 enqueues every resolved local link as an embedded artifact and re-walks it (driven by storage/artifact_discovery.rs:52-73), so one root citing a documentation hub pulls the whole cross-linked set in. 7 of 24 containers produce 675 of the 684 copies. lead_notes.subject: lead shell cwd drifted into a worker worktree and wrote .jit there
lead_notes.detail: After `cd .agents/worktrees/agent-2ac35e8e && git merge main`, the Bash tool's cwd persisted. Every later command ran in that worktree. `jit issue update f2cac2bd --state done` transitioned the issue inside the WORKTREE's .jit, and the follow-up `jit issue status` read the worktree's .jit — where the wave-5 gate runs do not exist, because .jit/gate-runs records are tracked but the new ones were not yet committed, so a worktree checked out at 36defd8a has none of them. The reported symptom was alarming and completely false: every wave-5 gate appeared to revert from passed/failed to pending and ~2h of gate evidence looked deleted. Nothing was lost; main was intact throughout. The tell was `git reflog` showing the worker branch's history instead of main's, and the worktree carrying the same two modified .jit files main appeared to carry.
lead_notes.decision: Reverted the two stray files in the worktree with `git checkout --` before its rework worker could commit them, and notified that worker. Use `git -C <path>` for worktree git operations rather than `cd`, since it never mutates the shell's cwd. For `jit`, which has no -C equivalent, prefix the command with an explicit `cd /home/vkaskivuo/Projects/just-in-time &&` every time. Before trusting any surprising .jit reading, run `pwd` first. This is the session-2 trap recurring in the same session that recorded it.

lead_notes.subject: the stale-binary guard is narrower than sessions 1-2 assumed
lead_notes.detail: crates/jit/src/domain/build_provenance.rs refuses a verdict only when binary identity is established AND either the build was dirty or a DECLARED BUILD-INPUT path changed. BINARY_BUILD_INPUTS is Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, crates/jit/Cargo.toml, crates/jit/Cargo.lock, crates/jit/build.rs, crates/jit/src/, profiles/jit-dogfood/, scripts/hooks/pre-commit, scripts/hooks/pre-push. A bare HEAD move past the build commit is NOT staleness.
lead_notes.decision: Reinstall only when a commit since the build touched one of those paths. Wave 7 DID touch crates/jit/src/ (d2870182), so a reinstall is required here. Wave 8's archive executions write only dev/ and .jit/, neither a build input, so the 24 sequential runs should not each need a reinstall — verify empirically at the first sweep rather than assuming, and fall back to reinstalling per commit if a verdict is refused.

lead_notes.subject: a dirty working tree of non-build-input paths does not invalidate a gate verdict
lead_notes.detail: Gates 2-5 of the wave-8 batch ran while the tree carried an uncommitted dev/active/8e071e18-dev-artifact-layout/handoff-3.md and a modified dev/active/8e071e18-progress.json. All four passed and recorded tree_dirty: true. This confirms ONLY the dirty-tree half of N8. The moved-HEAD half is still a code reading: both batches this session ran with the binary's build commit exactly equal to HEAD, so a HEAD moved past the build commit was never exercised.
lead_notes.decision: Sessions 1-2's rule 'never edit any repo file while a gate batch runs' can be relaxed to 'never edit a BUILD-INPUT file while a gate batch runs' — progress files, handoffs, and dev/ artifacts are safe. Do NOT yet assume the moved-HEAD half: verify it on the FIRST archive sweep by committing the sweep and evaluating repo-validate without reinstalling. Refusal is exit 10 with reason commit_mismatch; on refusal, reinstall per sweep and correct N8.

lead_notes.subject: wave 8 now has an internal three-step ordering
lead_notes.detail: The 24 archive executions are no longer dispatchable directly. ac45f567 (anchor fragments) -> 0e5dff57 (retain out-of-root + bound discovery) -> the 24 sweeps. Both new tasks carry story:area-classification, so 35499d1e depends on 0e5dff57 and correctly demoted ready -> backlog when the edge landed (the known demotion bug 533da2df did not bite here). The sweeps were wired to 0e5dff57 only, with --reduce: the edge to ac45f567 is transitively implied and adding it would fail validation.
lead_notes.decision: Dispatch ac45f567 first and alone; it is the only ready node of the three. Re-preview all 24 containers after 0e5dff57 lands - every sweep issue's stated relocation/copy counts predate both changes and will be wrong. Each sweep reads its own plan rather than a frozen list, which the issue bodies already require.

lead_notes.subject: execute the plan in a throwaway worktree before believing a preview
lead_notes.detail: A preview reporting eligible with zero blockers is NOT evidence that execution succeeds; eligibility skips the proposed-layout check entirely. `git worktree add --detach <scratch> HEAD` then running the real --execute inside it exposed 8 refusals that 24 clean previews had hidden, at zero risk: the main tree was untouched throughout and the probe was removed afterwards. It also produced the per-container copy census that answered E9.
lead_notes.decision: Before dispatching any wave whose issues are single pre-enumerated mutating commands, rehearse the whole wave in a detached probe worktree at HEAD and compare against the preview. Capture per-item stdout and stderr to SEPARATE FILES - a first attempt at this used `out=$(... ; echo "$out")` inside a loop, which reads the PREVIOUS iteration's variable and misattributed every error message. Exit codes were unaffected.

lead_notes.subject: installing with ANY uncommitted change makes the build dirty and the guard refuses
lead_notes.detail: cargo-ci was refused with exit 10, reason 'this jit binary predates the tree under review', because install-jit.sh ran while the lead's own `jit issue claim` was still uncommitted in .jit/. The guard reported 'built from commit 556b504f with a dirty working tree at build time'. .jit/ is NOT a declared build input, which is exactly why this is easy to get wrong.
lead_notes.decision: N9 covers a dirty tree at GATE time and remains correct: gates ran fine with dev/ artifacts uncommitted. This is the different case of a dirty tree at BUILD time, where the dirty flag is recorded into the binary's provenance and no later cleanup clears it. Sequence for every wave close: merge, commit EVERYTHING including .jit/, then install, then evaluate. Re-installing after committing cleared it and both gates passed.

lead_notes.subject: real-data measurement is necessary but not sufficient; it misses unexercised configuration paths
lead_notes.detail: The lead measured all 24 containers against the worker's branch and every criterion held: 175 moves with identical move SETS in 24/24, copies 684->20, artifacts 993->278, 0 blockers. code-review then found two blocking defects anyway. F1 lived on a path this repository never exercises - all 8 of its managed paths are inside dev/, so a managed-path carve-out on the out-of-root rule is inert here and would only harm an adopter. F2 was invisible to any check that inspects the resulting plan, because the plan was correct and only the read volume was wrong.
lead_notes.decision: Keep measuring real data - it is what caught the Copy-to-Move flip and what grounded both owner decisions - but never treat it as review. When a change keys on configuration, ask what this repository's configuration does NOT exercise, and read the diff for carve-outs that the local config makes inert.

lead_notes.subject: a superseding directive can lose a race with the worker it supersedes
lead_notes.detail: The lead sent a rework message directing F2, then learned from the worker's own delayed completion report that F2 costs 8 Copy-to-Move flips, then sent a hold, then an owner ruling amending REQ-03 so F2 was moot. The worker had already implemented F2 by the time the hold landed, and commit 4ab2213d shipped 183 moves - the exact outcome the owner declined. One full rework attempt was spent producing work that had to be reverted, and the counter is now at 2 of 2 for reasons unrelated to worker quality.
lead_notes.decision: Two changes. (1) When a worker's completion report is outstanding, do not dispatch rework until it arrives or is explicitly abandoned - the report is the cheapest source of exactly the constraint that invalidates the dispatch. (2) When an escalation is opened on a finding, tell the worker to HOLD that finding in the same message that opens the escalation, not in a follow-up. Do not let the rework counter penalise a worker for following a directive the lead later withdrew: on the next round, judge the work, and if a third round is needed escalate the counter's reset rather than the worker.

lead_notes.subject: encode the reason a tempting optimisation is refused, as a test
lead_notes.detail: Bounding evidence acquisition at the out-of-root frontier is an obvious improvement that reads as strictly better: it shrinks reads as well as plans. It is refused because the repository-wide ownership relation derives outside-owner evidence from chains that leave and re-enter the development root, so bounding it silently converts 8 artifacts from copy to relocation and deletes live files other issues' documents still reach. The worker implemented it twice, correctly reasoning both times, and reverted once on its own measurement.
lead_notes.decision: A doc comment saying 'deliberately unbounded' was not enough - it did not survive a reviewer asking for the opposite. Directed a regression test that fails if acquisition is bounded: an artifact whose only outside-owner claim arrives through an out-of-root hub must classify as Copy with outside-owner evidence. Generally: when a change is refused for a non-local reason, pin the reason with a test, not with prose.

lead_notes.subject: `git stash push <path>` then `git stash pop` around a merge can pop an unrelated stash
lead_notes.detail: The lead's merge ritual was: stash the uncommitted .jit claim, merge, pop. On the third merge the stash push was a NO-OP, because the claim had already been committed in the preceding step, so nothing was saved and no new stash entry was created. The pop then applied stash@{0}, a pre-existing unrelated WIP ('deletion bug investigation') left in this repository long before this session. It conflicted, leaving UU markers in crates/jit/src/storage/json.rs and integration_test.rs and foreign edits in two more files. Because the pop conflicted, git KEPT the stash entry, so nothing was destroyed.
lead_notes.decision: Recovered with `git reset --hard HEAD` back to the merge commit; all 3 pre-existing stashes intact and the merge itself verified uncontaminated (8 files, none of them json.rs). Stop using stash around merges entirely: commit the claim BEFORE merging, which N12 already requires for the install step anyway. If a stash is ever unavoidable, capture the ref from `git stash create` and apply that specific ref - never bare `pop`, which is positional and silently targets someone else's work when your own push was a no-op.

lead_notes.subject: verify a guard test is load-bearing by breaking what it guards, not by reading it
lead_notes.detail: The worker added the directed regression test and reported instrumenting two bounding variants to prove it fails under each. Rather than take that on trust or re-derive both variants, the lead ran a cheaper negative control in the worker's warm worktree: inject an early `return owners;` into discover_embedded_owners behind an env var, run the single test, observe it fail at exactly the reported assertion (archive.rs:1920, 'the claim reaching the target through the hub must survive'), then revert. That proves the assertion depends on the ownership walk - the mechanism actually at risk - in about two minutes against a warm target dir.
lead_notes.decision: For any test whose value is that it fails later, break the thing it guards and watch it fail before accepting it. Use the worker's already-built worktree for the experiment; a fresh probe worktree costs a full cold compile for the same answer.

lead_notes.subject: the leak check is dispatch-scoped and does not cover post-completion experiments
lead_notes.detail: check-leak-into-main.sh compares main against a snapshot taken at DISPATCH time and is run once after a wave completes. This leak happened after the issue's implementation was finished, while the worker ran a verification experiment at the lead's request, and would have been missed entirely had the worker not self-reported. An unexplained `dirty=true` at install time and an unexplained incremental-state gate failure were the only signals reaching the lead, and both have innocuous explanations that were accepted.
lead_notes.decision: Treat an unexplained dirty tree or a stale incremental directory as a possible concurrent writer, not only as a local transient - especially while any worker is still live. Re-run the leak check before every install and every gate batch, not only at wave close, and re-run it after directing a worker to perform any experiment. Directing a worker to instrument production code is what created the exposure; when a verification needs temporary source edits, prefer running it as the lead in a disposable probe worktree.

lead_notes.subject: the moved-HEAD half of N8 is now confirmed empirically
lead_notes.detail: repo-validate was evaluated for 84c4e956 with the installed binary built at 0eebad7d and HEAD at 389ca71f - two intervening commits, touching only .jit/ and dev/active/. The verdict was accepted (status passed) with no reinstall.
lead_notes.decision: N8's rule is fully verified in both halves: reinstall only when a commit since the build touched one of the nine BINARY_BUILD_INPUTS paths. A bare HEAD move is not staleness, and a dirty tree of non-build-input paths at GATE time is not either (N9). A dirty tree at BUILD time still is (N12). The 24 archive sweeps write only dev/ and .jit/, so one install covers the whole batch.

lead_notes.subject: a rehearsal must end in validation, not in exit codes
lead_notes.detail: N11's probe-worktree rehearsal was run as prescribed and all 48 commands (24 previews + 24 executions) exited 0 with empty stderr, which reads as a clean wave. Running `jit validate` inside the probe afterwards failed immediately on a dangling document reference. The defect is invisible to eligibility (all 24 eligible, zero blockers), to exit status (all 0), and to the plan's action counts (moves and copies are correct); only the post-state reveals it.
lead_notes.decision: Extend N11: after rehearsing a wave in the probe, run the project's own whole-repository validation inside the probe and diff the result against the pre-run state. For an archival wave also run `jit doc conformance` there. Exit codes describe the command, not the repository it left behind.

lead_notes.subject: a dispatch prompt asked for more than the criterion, and the worker caught it
lead_notes.detail: The dispatch prompt told the worker REQ-05 meant byte-level agreement of the whole quoted TOML block. The guide's excerpt is a trimmed teaching quote: it omits the template and node description strings and carries its own explanatory comments. Whole-block byte identity would mean pasting two long description strings into the guide and deleting its teaching comments - which the same prompt's scope boundary forbade. The worker made the plan-document declaration byte-identical, additionally proved value-level agreement for every key the excerpt declares (zero mismatches across template keys, anchors, anchor_edges, transforms and both nodes), and asked for the call rather than silently choosing.
lead_notes.decision: Accepted the worker's reading. The criterion says 'the declaration quoted in the guide matches the example registry it quotes' - what is quoted matches; omitted keys are not mismatches. The prompt was stricter than the contract, and the contract governs. This is not the no-argue discipline: that binds the lead when a REVIEWER cites a contract, not when the lead's own prompt overshoots one. Generally: when writing a dispatch prompt, quote the criterion rather than paraphrasing it into something tighter.

lead_notes.subject: a pitfall recorded as 'covered by a later issue' has now blocked an earlier review three times
lead_notes.detail: P2 blocked b3fc1a92 in wave 2 (E2). P4 and P5 were both recorded in waves 2 and 3 with the disposition 'covered by 4a6fb8c1 in wave 12, VERIFY there', and both came back as blocking doc-review findings on 89b5899a in wave 8 (E14). In every case the pitfall was correctly attributed - the later issue really does own the file - and in every case the attribution did not stop the finding.
lead_notes.decision: When a pitfall is a live adopter-facing falsehood rather than a missing improvement, 'covered by a later issue' is not a disposition, it is a scheduled review failure. On this epic the remaining ones to treat this way are P6 (issue_scoped_areas absent from the configuration reference, owned by 58c56743) and P17 (four adopter sites teaching the flat plan-doc pattern, owned by 8ff4cff3 - now landed on main). Check each against the surface of any issue about to be gated, and remediate ahead of the gate rather than after it.

lead_notes.subject: two consecutive Opus workers on the same issue died on API 529 before writing anything
lead_notes.detail: w-ca832358 and w-ca832358-r2 both failed with 'API Error: 529 Overloaded', 5-25 minutes in, each leaving a clean worktree with zero commits. The 8ff4cff3 worker on the same model completed normally in the same window, so this is capacity variance rather than anything about the task. The cost was ~35 minutes of wall clock on the epic's critical path, since every remaining wave sits behind ca832358.
lead_notes.decision: Third dispatch went to Sonnet, with the prompt strengthened on two axes: an explicit instruction to commit the failing test before the fix and the fix before verification, so a mid-task loss costs one step rather than the whole task; and an explicit warning that the PATH `jit` binary predates the branch, so a probe run must invoke a binary built from the worker's own change or it measures the old behaviour. Generally: for a task on the critical path, put the commit-early instruction in the prompt from the first dispatch, and treat a clean worktree after a failure as confirmation that nothing needs reconciling.

lead_notes.subject: a fresh-repository probe is the honest evidence for a shipped-default criterion
lead_notes.detail: 35499d1e REQ-01 and REQ-02 are about what a FRESHLY INITIALIZED repository does, which this repository's live .jit/ cannot evidence - the dogfooding boundary. Ran `git init` + `jit init` in a scratch directory with the installed binary: the scaffolded [documentation] table carries 8 managed paths, 6 permanent paths and 4 issue-scoped areas with no hand editing, and archival reports policy_status 'configured'. Then linked a deck at dev/presentations/deck.md to a task, terminalised it, and previewed both target forms: `jit archive document` gives eligible with 1 move and zero blockers, `jit archive container` gives eligible with destination dev/archive/b44aeed5 and zero blockers.
lead_notes.decision: Keep the scratch repository until the checkpoint closes and extend the same probe for REQ-03 and REQ-04 once ca832358 lands. The bare short-id destination in that probe is also live evidence for 89b5899a REQ-01's no-title-fallback clause on a repository that has never seen this epic's data.

lead_notes.subject: an archival plan is order-dependent, so a pre-computed action table is not evidence
lead_notes.detail: Measuring all 24 container plans against a PRISTINE tree gives 175 moves and 20 copies. Measuring them interleaved with their executions, in the run order, gives 176 and 19. The difference is one artifact: dev/active/json-output-standardization-plan.md has two owners, and container 14303b30 - first in the order - COPIES it and relinks the outside owner's reference to that copy. By the time 9d427a6b is previewed, only its inside owner remains, so the action is Move rather than Copy. Each execution relinks references and thereby changes later containers' ownership sets.
lead_notes.decision: Take each sweep's evidence from the preview computed immediately before that sweep executes, in the fixed order - which is what the sweep issue bodies already require ('the execution reads its own plan rather than a frozen list') and what the runner does. Never compare a pristine measurement against an interleaved one and read the difference as a regression; the lead nearly did exactly that.

lead_notes.subject: A/B the same command on the same state with the old and the new binary
lead_notes.detail: The worker's own before/after numbers came from two different repository states (its baseline was quoted from the issue description, measured at a different HEAD), which is what made the 175/20 vs 176/19 discrepancy look alarming. The decisive check was cheap: run all 24 previews against ONE unchanged tree twice, once with the installed binary and once with the worker's release build invoked by explicit path. Actions identical at 175/20/83; artifacts carrying a reference change went move 152->152, copy 13->13, retain 33->0.
lead_notes.decision: For any change whose effect is a delta in derived output, hold the input state fixed and vary only the binary. A worker's release build in its own warm worktree is directly runnable against main for read-only commands, so this costs one loop and no rebuild - and it proves the change touched nothing it should not, which a post-state measurement alone cannot.

lead_notes.subject: stop a gate batch when an early failure predicts a later one in the same batch
lead_notes.detail: 334bcd6f's doc-review failed on a sentence in docs/reference/cli-commands.md. 89b5899a's doc-review was queued two positions later in the same batch, and its REQ-01 is destination naming - the very subject of that sentence - so it would very likely have re-reported the same defect against a different issue. Stopping the batch cost about one minute of the in-flight 8ff4cff3 review; letting it run would have cost a 30-minute review round plus a spurious failed-gate record on the checkpoint.
lead_notes.decision: When a batched gate fails, check the remaining entries for a shared surface before letting the batch continue. Fix, then restart the batch from the top.

lead_notes.subject: a criterion that can only be observed once needs its observation committed
lead_notes.detail: ca832358's REQ-05 was an end-to-end property of THIS repository: whole-repository validation passing after every terminal container plan executes. It had been verified twice - by the worker and independently by the lead - and code-review still failed it as 'materially unverified', correctly: no attributable test or recorded evidence existed in the repository. cargo-ci cannot establish it, and a fixture cannot either, because the criterion names this repository's own containers.
lead_notes.decision: Produce the observation as a committed artifact in the issue's OWN canonical directory (jit doc dir <issue> dev/active, not the epic's, or jit doc conformance reports it as misplaced), carrying the reproduction commands, a per-container table with exit status, and the verbatim validator output. Generally: when a criterion can only be observed by running something destructive once, the deliverable is the recorded observation, and the issue should say so at planning time rather than leaving a reviewer to discover the gap.

lead_notes.subject: three verification oracles, each wrong in a different way, before the right one
lead_notes.detail: Verifying that a RETAINED artifact was left alone took three attempts. (1) `os.path.exists(src)` failed on dev/reference/configuration.md, an embedded link target that never existed - correctly retained as a no-op and correctly non-blocking, because only an explicitly-linked source raises MissingSource. (2) Keying on content_identity failed too: the planner records an identity only for an artifact it will write, so it is null both for a present out-of-root file and for an absent one. (3) The right oracle is git: a sweep commits only after verification, so HEAD is the pre-run state and `git status --porcelain -- <path>` empty means the run left the path alone, whether or not it existed.
lead_notes.decision: When verifying that an operation left something untouched, compare the tree against its own previous committed state rather than inferring the previous state from the operation's own report. The report describes what the operation intended, not what was there.

lead_notes.subject: a per-run assertion does not survive being applied to the final tree
lead_notes.detail: Re-checking all 24 runs at the end flagged 14303b30 for a mirrored artifact absent at its source. It was correct per-run and correct at the end: dev/active/json-output-standardization-plan.md is owned by two issues, 14303b30 mirrors it and retains the source, and 9d427a6b - later in the order - relocates it, because the outside owner has by then been relinked to the mirrored copy so only the inside owner remains. Both archived copies exist, the live source is gone, both references resolve.
lead_notes.decision: A retrospective pass over a sequence of mutations must model the sequence. Index every later relocation before asserting an earlier run's retention, and assert the bytes survived at the later destination instead. Recorded in the evidence record so the apparent contradiction is answered where a reader meets it.

lead_notes.subject: a stale in-content citation is a shared surface, so the issue that owns it should not wait its turn
lead_notes.detail: docs-mechanical's M3 citation check failed on 35499d1e because two adopter guides cited dev/design/worktree-parallel-work.md, which a sweep had relocated. That gate is carried by many issues, so the stale citation was failing a check for the whole remaining epic rather than for one issue. 623e4c46 owned exactly those two citations and 834a78a8 owned five more in Rust sources; both were blocked behind aa38b236, whose consolidated warning list they do not actually need because each enumerates its own citations.
lead_notes.decision: Rewired both onto the sweeps that moved their targets - 60c398d3 and deb50576, both Done - rather than onto aa38b236, and ran them immediately. That is reordering, not rescoping: no criterion changed, and both issues are written to be satisfied by the citation RESOLVING rather than by that issue having edited it. Both passed every gate first try. Generally: when a gate fails on repository state that a later issue owns, check whether that issue's stated dependency is a real prerequisite or a convenience before creating a remediation task.

lead_notes.subject: an enumeration decided at planning time is a hypothesis, not evidence
lead_notes.detail: The five disposition issues each enumerated their files with the disposition decided at planning time, and D-20 calls those outcomes 'decided at planning time and executed without judgement'. Verified against the tree, SIX of 72 assertions were false, all on mirrored rows: two files enumerated as mirrored to seven directories each were never planned by any run and no copy exists; two more named 8 destinations and had 2 and 1; two were enumerated as mirrored with the source retained when the run had moved them. Across those rows the enumerations named 22 mirror destinations of which 20 hold no copy. Recording any of them as enumerated would have falsified 66c467c1 REQ-03 or 93aaa2b2 REQ-03.
lead_notes.decision: Dispatch an enumeration-driven issue with verification as the primary instruction and transcription as the failure mode, naming one known mismatch so the worker has the shape. 'Executed without judgement' describes the command, not the record: the plan's own numbers drifted between planning and execution, and only the tree settles it. The same caution applies to the two issue descriptions whose background prose still states pre-run counts; no criterion asserts a count, so they were left as written.
